extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and educated readers of American government and constitutional law
extracted.subtask_description: A close, practical study of the organization, methods, and real balance of power of the U.S. Congress as the working center of the national government rather than the Constitution's theoretical balances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground study of Congress to understand the Constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Any one who is unfamiliar with what Congress actually does and how it does it ... is very far from a knowledge of the constitutional system under which we live.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that to know the Constitution to-day one must study Congress's actual practices, duties, occupations, devices of management, and resources of power; theoretical balances are largely ideal and inadequate without this empirical study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess practical balance of power empirically
rubrics_metrics.description: The balances of the Constitution are for the most part only ideal. For all practical purposes the national government is supreme over the state governments, and Congress predominant over its so-called coordinate branches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating constitutional functioning, prioritize observed power and practice (e.g., how often Congress controls executive operations) over textual or theoretical distributions of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine standing committees as centers of initiative and control
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress very early divided itself into standing committees which it equipped with very comprehensive and thorough-going privileges of legislative initiative and control, and set itself through these to administer the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus analysis on standing committees: their privileges, initiative, control over legislation and administration, and how committee organization enables Congress to 'enter more and more into the details of administration.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Appraise congressional expansion as result of organization and efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: The enlarged powers of Congress are the fruits rather of an immensely increased efficiency of organization, and of the redoubled activity consequent upon the facility of action secured by such organization, than of any definite and persistent scheme of conscious usurpation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging congressional growth, consider institutional changes (division of labor, committee procedures, capacity for detailed work) rather than attributing expansion solely to deliberate usurpation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Senate's overt semi-executive claims from House practices
rubrics_metrics.description: It is only in the exercise of those functions of public and formal consultation and cooperation with the President which are the peculiar offices of the Senate, that the power of Congress has made itself offensive to popular conceptions of constitutional propriety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the Senate separately by looking at treaty ratification and confirmations (executive sessions), where its claims to power are demonstrative and more visible; use cases like the St. Thomas treaty and the Alabama claims for illustration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge presidential power by both formal prerogatives and practical capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: In legal theory the President can control every operation of every department of the executive branch ... but in fact it is not practicable for him to do so, and a limitation of fact is as potent as a prohibition of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the presidency not just by constitutional text (prerogatives, veto, removal) but by practical constraints (size of administration, delegation to Secretaries, selection processes) that reduce effective control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate the role and limits of the Cabinet and Secretaries
rubrics_metrics.description: The members of the President's cabinet have always been prominent in administration ... but they were then only the President's advisers, whereas they are now rather the President's colleagues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how cabinet members function in practice (advisers vs. independent executives), and how Congress' investigatory and management habits may make Secretaries 'humble servants' of congressional committees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical incidents to test constitutional bearings
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not often easy to see the true constitutional bearing of strictly legislative action; but it is patent even to the least observant that in the matter of appointments ... senators have often outrun their legal right ... by insisting upon being first consulted concerning nominations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply concrete historical episodes (e.g., Tenure-of-Office Act, St. Thomas treaty, Alabama claims) to test claims about constitutional practice and to reveal shifts in inter-branch relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the multiplicity of House leaders (committee chairmen)
rubrics_metrics.description: The leaders of the House are the chairmen of the principal Standing Committees. Indeed ... the House has as many leaders as there are subjects of legislation ... the House is guided by a special leader in the person of the chairman of the Standing Committee charged with the superintendence of measures of the particular class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying the House, give attention to committee chairmen as the effective leaders for legislative classes, and to the decentralization this produces (many-headed leadership rather than a unified ministry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate the Speaker with active legislative leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: The Speaker of the House of Representatives stands as near to leadership as any one; but his will does not run as a formative and imperative power in legislation much beyond the appointment of the committees ... he is a great party chief, but the hedging circumstances of his official position as presiding officer prevent his performing the part of active leadership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analysis, treat the Speaker's role as important but limited—appointing committees and smoothing party paths—rather than as equivalent to a parliamentary prime minister or ministry leader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize practical obstacles facing new members; procedural knowledge matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The newly-elected member ... experiences great difficulty in adjusting his preconceived ideas ... his bill is doubtless ready for presentation early in the session ... he finds getting the floor an arduous and precarious undertaking ... he learns that his only safe day ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When advising or evaluating congressional behavior, account for the steep learning curve of new members: knowledge of rules, customs, 'regular order', unanimous consent practices, committee referral, and routinized means of obtaining the floor is essential for effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider veto power as essentially legislative in effect
rubrics_metrics.description: In the exercise of his power of veto, which is of course, beyond all comparison, his most formidable prerogative, the President acts not as the executive but as a third branch of the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing the President's role in lawmaking and balance of powers, treat veto usage as part of legislative bargaining and balance, especially effective only under certain party conditions (e.g., even party balances or weak majorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate national government capacity before extending federal responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: It becomes a matter of the utmost importance ... to examine critically the government upon which this new weight of responsibility and power seems likely to be cast, in order that its capacity both for the work it now does and for that which it may be called upon to do may be definitely estimated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy decisions about centralizing additional national functions (commerce regulation, corporate control, fiscal arrangements) should be preceded by practical assessment of Congress's methods, administrative apparatus, and overall capacity to discharge new duties.
